strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale (421,363 samples) multimodal dataset pairing raw 4D ERA5 reanalysis data with textual severe weather warnings across China, covering seven severe weather types plus normal conditions, which is larger and more temporally precise (hourly, 12-hour windows without averaging) than several prior datasets summarized in Table 1.

Proposes three plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) targeting temporal, spatial, and channel/vertical dimensions of 4D meteorological data, addressing a real limitation of existing MLLMs that flatten or subsample pressure levels.
Reasonably thorough ablation study (Table 3) showing incremental and complementary contributions of the three modules across multiple QA tasks.

Interpretability analysis (weight visualizations in Figs. 6, 8, 9) provides some physical plausibility checks, e.g., 125 hPa wind sensitivity, red-warning temporal weighting in early hours, which is a nice touch connecting model behavior to known meteorological understanding.
Diverse QA task design (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) spanning different granularities and reasoning types adds practical value and enables multi-faceted evaluation of model capability.
Comparison against a closed-source baseline (GPT-4o) usefully motivates the need for specialized architectures for this data type.
weaknesses: Overall performance remains weak in absolute terms even for the best model (e.g., MC-sub only 58.19, NSW only 2.1/5), raising concerns about practical readiness and whether the reported gains reflect genuine capability versus large room for improvement not yet closed; the paper does not sufficiently discuss why NSW performance is so poor despite "substantial" claimed gains over GPT-4o (an extremely weak baseline).

The GPT-4o baseline comparison is not a fair or informative apples-to-apples comparison: GPT-4o is only given 4 variables compressed into 3 channels without fine-tuning or the proposed modules, while all reported MMLM results already include the three modules baked in — there is no reported baseline of the open-source backbones WITHOUT the plug-and-play modules against GPT-4o, and no zero-shot vs fine-tuned distinction is clarified, making the magnitude of module contribution vs. simply fine-tuning on the new dataset hard to disentangle from Table 2 alone.

Data leakage/temporal alignment risk: using a 12-hour window starting at the warning issuance time [t, t+11] as model input while predicting/describing the same warning issued at time t is arguably diagnosis/nowcasting of the current warning rather than "prediction," since some or most of the 12-hour window meteorological data used as input temporally overlaps with or follows the moment the warning was already issued; the paper repeatedly frames this as "prediction" which appears to overstate the task's forecasting nature.

The dataset's severity/quality control is unclear: automatic GPT-4o scoring for NSW is used both as an evaluation metric and is somewhat circular (an LLM judging LLM outputs against ground truth with a coarse 0-5 rubric), and no human validation of GPT-4o's grading is reported.

No comparison to more directly relevant strong meteorological foundation models (e.g., Aardvark/Bodnar's Aurora, GraphCast-style baselines) or ablation isolating gains purely from fine-tuning vs. architectural modules; the improvement of modules over vanilla fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL is not directly shown (Table 3 baseline is 42.73 MC-main without modules vs. 72.37 with modules and presumably fine-tuning in Table 2 — inconsistent numbers between Table 2 and Table 3 for the same backbone are confusing and not reconciled).
The dataset covers only 2 years (2023-2024) restricted to China, limiting geographic and climatological generalizability claims despite the "nationwide, year-round" framing.

Text warnings are extremely templated (fixed categorical fields: location, weather type, severity level), so the "language generation" aspect is closer to structured classification/extraction than open-ended severe weather understanding, which weakens the novelty claim of deep textual interpretation.

Presentation issues: inconsistent figure/module naming in Fig. 2 caption vs. text (TGF/GCA/TGS vs. DTGF/TGS/TGCA), a typo/error in module naming (Fig 2 caption swaps names), and unclear description of how the modules' individual outputs are concatenated and fused with the vision encoder in the main architecture.

Severe class imbalance (e.g., snow storm only ~1.5-2% of data) is acknowledged but not effectively addressed via reweighting, oversampling, or class-specific analysis beyond noting the issue, undermining the claimed general applicability of the dataset/method across all severe weather types.

Ablation and main results only report accuracy without confidence intervals, statistical significance testing, or multiple-run variance, hampering assessment of robustness of the reported gains, especially given the modest sample size (5,000) used for ablation relative to the full dataset.

strengths: MP-Bench is a large-scale (421,363 samples), nationwide, multi-year (2023-2024), multi-category (7 severe weather types + normal) multimodal dataset pairing raw 4D ERA5 reanalysis fields with official CMA textual warnings, which is a genuinely useful resource compared to prior datasets that rely on daily-averaged or spatially/temporally limited data (Table 1 comparison is informative).

The four QA task formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) with varying spatial granularity and answer complexity provide a reasonably rich benchmark suite for evaluating multimodal reasoning over meteorological data.

The three proposed modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are plug-and-play and the ablation study (Table 3) demonstrates each contributes incremental gains and that their combination is complementary, with some interpretability analysis (Fig. 6, appendix Figs. 8-9) linking learned weights to physically plausible patterns (e.g., higher temporal weights shortly after red-warning issuance, sensitivity peaks at physically relevant pressure levels).

The paper is transparent about limitations in the conclusion (misclassified samples show more complex fields) and provides substantial appendix detail (QA prompt templates, hyperparameters, scoring rubric) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The temporal alignment strategy is questionable for the paper's central framing as 'prediction': meteorological data are extracted from the window [t, t+11] starting AT the warning issuance time t, meaning the model has access to data concurrent with and after the warning was already manually issued by human forecasters. This raises concern that the task is closer to post-hoc description/nowcasting of already-known events rather than genuine early prediction, undermining the paper's core motivation of an 'early-warning' AI system; this is not adequately discussed or justified.

The comparison against GPT-4o (Table 2) is methodologically confounded: GPT-4o is evaluated zero-shot with a simplified 3-channel input (2 variables + derived wind), while the 'open-source' models are LoRA fine-tuned AND already equipped with the proposed DTGF/TGS/TGCA modules. This conflates the contribution of fine-tuning, architecture choice, and the proposed modules, so the large reported gains over GPT-4o cannot be attributed specifically to the proposed method's novelty; a fairer comparison (e.g., fine-tuned baselines without the proposed modules against GPT-4o, and against the same open-source backbones without modules) is missing from the main results.

Absolute performance on the hardest and arguably most operationally relevant task (NSW, nationwide free-form structured description) remains very poor (best score only 2.1/5, i.e., ~42%), and accuracy on rare-but-critical severe weather types such as snow storm is extremely low (≤6% in Fig. 5) due to class imbalance, which is not adequately addressed by the proposed method and raises concerns about real-world operational usefulness for exactly the tail-risk events that matter most for disaster mitigation.

The technical novelty of the three modules is modest: DTGF is a fairly standard gated temporal fusion based on frame differences, TGS is essentially coordinate-based Gaussian spatial weighting (not truly 'text-driven' beyond coordinate extraction from text), and TGCA is a form of channel/text cross-attention; these are incremental adaptations of well-established attention/gating mechanisms to a new domain rather than fundamentally new architectural contributions.

NSW evaluation relies entirely on GPT-4o as an automated judge with no validation against human ratings or inter-annotator agreement, introducing potential bias/noise into a key reported metric without any reliability analysis.

There is inconsistency between module names across the manuscript (e.g., Figure 2 caption lists 'TGF, GCA, and TGS' while the text and other tables use 'DTGF, TGS, TGCA'), and the ablation study uses a different, smaller (5,000-sample) evaluation subset than the main Table 2 results, making direct comparison across tables difficult and reducing overall clarity/rigor of the presentation.

No comparison is provided against existing specialized nowcasting/NWP-based severe weather models or other multimodal weather benchmarks' reported baselines beyond the four chosen general-purpose VLM backbones, limiting the ability to contextualize how meaningful the reported gains are relative to the broader state of the art in severe weather prediction.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale (421,363 pairs) nationwide, year-round multimodal dataset for severe weather that preserves full 4D meteorological structure (time × pressure level × lat × lon) rather than collapsing to daily-averaged or RGB-projected inputs, addressing a genuine gap versus prior datasets such as CLLMate, WeatherQA, and ClimateIQA.

The three proposed plug-and-play modules (DTGF for temporal gating, TGS for text-driven geographic spatial masking, TGCA for text-driven channel/pressure-level attention) are individually motivated by physical reasoning and are shown to be complementary through a thorough ablation table (Table 3), with the full combination giving the largest gains across all five tasks.

Comparative evaluation against a closed-source model (GPT-4o) and four open-source MLLM backbones provides useful evidence that generic MLLMs struggle with raw high-dimensional meteorological data, motivating the need for specialized fusion modules.

Interpretability analysis (weight visualizations in Fig. 6/8/9) shows module attention patterns that are physically plausible (e.g., higher wind-speed sensitivity at 125 hPa, elevated temporal weights in the hours following red-level warnings), lending some qualitative validation beyond raw accuracy numbers.

The dataset design includes four QA formats spanning different granularities (region-level to national-scale, category-only to category+severity), which broadens potential downstream utility beyond a single benchmark task.
weaknesses: Performance on the most demanding, arguably most practically relevant task (NSW, nationwide free-form warning generation) remains extremely low (max 2.1/5), and snow storm classification accuracy is near-chance (≤6%) for all models, indicating the method is far from a viable end-to-end warning system despite the framing in the abstract/introduction.

Table 2 reports only the modules-augmented versions of the four backbone MLLMs; no unmodified baseline numbers are shown for LLaVA-NeXT-Video, Video-LLaVA, or InternVL3, so it is not possible to verify how much of the reported improvement is attributable to the proposed modules versus backbone choice for three of the four models (only Qwen2.5-VL has a full ablation in Table 3).

The GPT-4o comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: GPT-4o receives only 3 aggregated channels (via u/v synthesis) while MMLM ingests full 4D/185-channel data, which likely inflates the apparent necessity of the proposed architecture rather than isolating the effect of the fusion modules themselves.

Potential circularity/leakage concern: since CMA warnings are themselves issued partly based on interpretation of reanalysis-like meteorological fields, the paper does not discuss whether the ERA5-derived features used as input could trivially correlate with warning labels in ways that overstate real forecasting difficulty versus classification of already-implied conditions.

Reproducibility is limited by underspecified architectural details (e.g., exact vision encoder processing of the 4D tensor, resolution/grid size actually fed to the model, how the three module outputs are concatenated and reduced to LLM input dimension) and by results being reported from single runs without variance/confidence intervals.

The claim of being the "first" MLLM to interpret raw meteorological data into warning text is somewhat overstated given existing multimodal weather/climate QA systems (CLLMate, WeatherQA, ClimateIQA) already perform related event description and reasoning tasks, even if MP-Bench's data fidelity is higher.

Dataset and evaluation are restricted to China with two years of data (2023 train, 2024 test), leaving open questions about geographic and temporal generalization of both the dataset and the proposed modules.

Minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., inconsistent module abbreviations between text and figures — DTGF/TGF, TGCA/GCA — and several typographical errors) slightly hinder readability, though these are correctable presentation issues rather than substantive flaws.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale (421,363 pairs) multimodal dataset pairing raw, high-temporal-resolution (hourly, 12h window) and high-vertical-resolution (37 pressure levels x 5 variables) ERA5 data with textual severe weather warnings across 7 event types nationwide in China, filling a real gap relative to prior datasets that rely on daily-averaged or coarsely compressed inputs.

Proposes three physically motivated, plug-and-play fusion modules (DTGF for temporal gating, TGS for text-driven spatial Gaussian masking, TGCA for text-driven channel/vertical attention) that are modular and can be attached to multiple off-the-shelf MLLM backbones.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: comparison against a closed-source zero-shot baseline (GPT-4o), four open-source MLLM backbones with and without the proposed modules, an ablation over module combinations, a temporal-window-length ablation, and a cross-regional generalization test on NOAA (US) data.

Interpretability analysis linking learned DTGF temporal weights and TGCA channel weights to known synoptic meteorological criteria (e.g., CMA warning issuance thresholds, classical pressure-level significance for gales/temperature/humidity), which lends some physical plausibility to the learned representations beyond pure benchmark numbers.

Four well-designed QA task types (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) spanning different granularities and difficulty levels, useful for probing different aspects of model understanding, with a reasonably documented LLM-as-judge scoring rubric for open-ended answers.
weaknesses: The framing as 'prediction' is questionable: the meteorological input window [t, t+11] is defined starting at the warning issuance time itself, meaning the model is given data concurrent with (or after) the moment human forecasters already identified and issued the warning, rather than data strictly prior to event onset. This raises concerns about whether the task is genuine forecasting/early-warning versus post-hoc classification/nowcasting, which is inconsistent with the stated motivation of providing 'timely' early warnings before human interpretation.

Absolute performance remains low across most metrics even for the best model+module combination (e.g., MC-sub Macro-F1 of 29.31, NSW score of 2.1/5, many Macro-F1 scores under 50), indicating the tasks are far from solved and that practical deployment readiness is unclear; the paper does not sufficiently discuss what performance level would be operationally meaningful.

The GPT-4o comparison is not a fair like-for-like baseline: it is zero-shot/unfine-tuned and restricted to only 3 aggregated channels, while all other 'baseline' and 'MMLM' models are LoRA fine-tuned on the target data; this makes the reported gap primarily an artifact of fine-tuning rather than a demonstration of GPT-4o's inherent inability to process meteorological data.

No comparison against non-MLLM specialized baselines (e.g., physics-based severe weather nowcasting systems, CNN/Transformer classifiers directly trained on gridded meteorological fields, or existing MLLM datasets' released models) is provided, making it hard to judge whether the added complexity of an MLLM pipeline provides real advantage over simpler, more efficient discriminative models for this classification-style task.

The three proposed modules, while domain-adapted, are architecturally fairly standard mechanisms (gating based on frame differences, Gaussian spatial masking keyed to coordinates, text-conditioned channel attention); the technical novelty relative to existing gating/attention literature is incremental, and the fusion layer (described only briefly as a 'learnable 3D convolution') lacks sufficient architectural detail for reproducibility.

No variance/error bars are reported despite the appendix stating results are averaged over three runs, limiting the ability to assess whether reported improvements (e.g., ablation deltas of a few points) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

The 'normal weather' negative sampling procedure (49,660 samples) is described only briefly, without clear justification of how negatives were chosen to avoid trivial spatial/temporal shortcuts, which is important given known imbalance and potential shortcut-learning risks in severe-weather classification.

The LLM-as-judge (GPT-4o) evaluation for NSW is not validated against human expert judgments in the manuscript, raising reliability concerns for this qualitative-yet-quantified metric, especially given GPT-4o's demonstrated poor domain understanding in the zero-shot severe-weather task shown earlier in the same paper.
Cross-regional generalization is tested on only 1,000 NOAA samples in an MC-only setting, a fairly narrow evaluation given the claimed geographic generalization contribution.

strengths: MP-Bench represents a substantial data-engineering effort: nationwide, multi-year (2023-2024), hourly-resolution ERA5 fields paired with 421,363 CMA warning records spanning seven severe-weather categories plus normal conditions, which is larger and more temporally/spatially comprehensive than several prior text-only or remote-sensing-only datasets listed in Table 1.
The four QA task formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) provide reasonable task diversity, moving beyond single-label classification toward structured, nationwide generation tasks.

The ablation study (Table 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 7-8) attempts physical interpretability by linking learned DTGF temporal weights and TGCA channel weights to CMA warning criteria and known synoptic features (e.g., 500 hPa wind, near-surface gale flow), which is a nice qualitative sanity check beyond raw accuracy numbers.

The paper includes a reasonably broad set of baselines (4 open-source MLLMs, 1 closed-source) and additional analyses (temporal window length, cross-geographic generalization to NOAA data, case study of failure modes), showing effort toward thorough empirical characterization.
weaknesses: Central framing problem: the model is trained and evaluated using ERA5 *reanalysis* data from the window [t, t+11] hours *starting at* the warning issuance time, i.e., data concurrent with or after the event the model is supposed to 'predict.' ERA5 reanalysis is not available in real time (it is produced with a substantial operational lag) and already encodes the atmospheric state during/after the warned event. This makes the task closer to retrospective classification/diagnosis of an already-occurred atmospheric state than genuine forecasting, which undermines the paper's repeated framing as an 'AI weather station' or 'forecasting' system deployable for early warning.

The comparison in Table 2 between 'Baseline' (3-channel input) and 'MMLM' (185-channel input + three modules) confounds the effect of input information volume with the effect of the proposed architectural modules. No ablation isolates the gain purely from exposing the model to 185 channels without the proposed fusion modules, so the attribution of improvement specifically to DTGF/TGS/TGCA (as opposed to simply richer input) is not well supported.

Absolute performance remains weak even for the best configuration: MC-sub Macro-F1 of 29.31 (out of 100) and an NSW LLM-judged score of 2.1 (out of 5) are far from levels that would support practical, automated warning issuance, which is in tension with the paper's claims of 'strong performance' and being 'a key step toward automated, AI-driven' forecasting.

Architectural details are underspecified: it is unclear how the outputs of DTGF/TGS/TGCA (operating on the raw 4D gridded meteorological tensor) are reconciled with the 'Vision Encoder' component shown in Fig. 2(a), which in the underlying MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, etc.) is pretrained on natural RGB images; how a 185-channel physical field is made compatible with this encoder is not explained. Additionally, Eq. (9) ('SigmoidSoftmax(VP^T)P') and the surrounding dimensional bookkeeping are notationally unclear/inconsistent, raising questions about correctness as written.

Evaluation design has a potential conflict of interest: GPT-4o is used both as the compared closed-source baseline model (shown to perform very poorly) and as the automatic judge for scoring the proposed model's NSW outputs, without discussion of judge bias or cross-validation against human raters.

Geographic and climatic coverage is narrow (China-only training data), and the cross-regional generalization test is limited to 1,000 NOAA samples evaluated only as a coarse multi-class task; this is insufficient to substantiate claims of general applicability as a worldwide 'AI weather station' concept.

Despite stating results are 'averaged over three independent runs,' no variance, standard deviation, or statistical significance is reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix, making it difficult to assess whether reported gains (e.g., ablation differences of 1-2 points) are robust or within noise.

strengths: Introduces MP-Bench, a large-scale (421,363 pairs), nationwide, multi-year multimodal dataset pairing raw 4D ERA5 meteorological fields (5 variables × 37 pressure levels, hourly resolution) with textual severe-weather warnings across 7 event types, avoiding the heavy temporal/vertical averaging used by prior datasets (Table 1 comparison is informative and the dataset appears to fill a genuine gap).

The four QA task formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW) span multiple granularities (regional to national) and reasoning styles (classification to open-ended generation), which usefully diversifies the benchmark's utility for downstream evaluation.

The three proposed plug-and-play modules (DTGF, TGS, TGCA) are lightweight, model-agnostic, and target well-motivated aspects of the data (temporal abruptness, geographic focus from text, channel/vertical redundancy); ablations (Table 3) show consistent, individually positive contributions and best performance when combined.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental protocol: comparison against a closed-source MLLM (GPT-4o) and four open-source backbones, an ablation on temporal window length, and a cross-geographical generalization test on NOAA Storm Events data.

Good qualitative/physical interpretability analysis connecting learned attention weights (e.g., TGCA emphasizing 500 hPa wind, DTGF emphasizing recent hours for red-level warnings) to established CMA warning criteria and synoptic meteorology, which strengthens the credibility of the proposed mechanisms beyond pure metric gains.
Reasonably thorough appendix with training/evaluation hyperparameters, dataset statistics, and prompt templates, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Task framing concern: the meteorological input window is [t, t+11] where t is the warning issuance time, i.e., the model is given data spanning the warning period itself rather than only data preceding the warning. This makes the task closer to concurrent detection/interpretation of an already-unfolding event than genuine forward prediction/early warning, which somewhat undercuts the paper's central framing as a "severe weather event prediction" or "early warning" system. This should be explicitly discussed/justified, or the framing softened.

Absolute performance remains modest even for the best model (e.g., MC-sub Macro-F1 ~29%, NSW score 2.1/5), which limits the paper's claim that MMLM represents a strong step toward practical automated warning systems; more discussion of failure modes and remaining gap to operational usefulness would help contextualize the contribution.

The ablation study (Table 3) and temporal-window study (Table 4/Table 7) use only a 5,000-sample subset rather than the full test set used in the main comparison (Table 2), creating an inconsistency in evaluation scale that makes it harder to directly connect ablation conclusions to the headline results, and raises questions about statistical robustness of the reported gains.

The NSW evaluation relies on GPT-4o as an LLM-judge, yet the same paper demonstrates GPT-4o performs very poorly at understanding meteorological data/severe weather text alignment (Section 5.3.1). This raises a potential circularity/reliability concern for using GPT-4o as a judge on a closely related task; no human validation of the LLM-judge scores is reported.

Dataset temporal coverage is limited to two years (2023 train / 2024 test) from a single country (China), and class distribution is heavily imbalanced (Gale ~42%, several classes <5%); combined with the fairly small (1,000-sample) and simplified (MC-main only) NOAA cross-region test, the claims of strong generalization and broad applicability are only lightly supported.

No comparison to physically grounded NWP-based nowcasting/classification baselines (non-MLLM) is provided, making it hard to assess whether the MLLM approach offers real advantages over simpler, established meteorological classification pipelines beyond producing natural-language output.

Increasing input channels from 3 to 185 substantially increases computational cost, but the paper provides no analysis of training/inference efficiency or scalability trade-offs introduced by the full 4D input and added modules.
